Bellsack’s central idea is: the game world is a mutable, high-dimensional vector, while the visible 3D terrain is the zero surface of a GPU-computed scalar field.

## Core model

- Each scalar in the world is a `Var`.
- A `Var` normally has:
  - `.p`: position/value/existence weight
  - `.v`: velocity
  - physics fields such as gradient, acceleration multiplier, damping, spring target, and bounds
  - named child Vars
- All Vars form one tree rooted at `v`; the current room is `q = v.Bellsack.Room1`.
- Each terrain parameter—position, radius, strength, and species-specific values—is another coordinate in the larger state vector.
- Var physics is sparse: only changed or interacting Vars enter the dirty queue and get integrated.

The result is more than moving fixed meshes. A collision can change the terrain’s parameters, so the terrain can deform in the restricted ways its mathematical species permits.

## Shapes and terrain

A species is an immutable, content-addressed pure GLSL function. Examples currently include:

- Bell5
- torus
- Mandelbulb
- rounded box
- capsule
- cone
- gyroid
- helix
- twisted torus
- knot tube
- lattice

Each instance of a species is called a wave. A wave supplies values such as its center, bounding radius, weight, and any custom function parameters.

At a sampled 3D position, Bellsack evaluates the nearby waves and sums their weighted density contributions:

- positive density: inside solid terrain
- negative density: open space
- zero density: the visible/collidable isosurface

`GlDag` gives GLSL functions content-derived names and tracks their dependencies. A `Zoo` is a set of species compiled together into the density shader. The current Loop B density ABI has 16 runtime species-loop slots.

The generated starter world currently contains 800 terrain waves across 10 selected species and 448 balls.

## GPU layer: Lamgl

Lamgl turns WebGL2 fragment shaders into a general tensor-compute API:

- A JavaScript call supplies tensor shape, GLSL source, uniforms, and input tensors.
- The call returns immutable tensors backed by float WebGL textures.
- Those tensors can feed later GPU calls without returning through the CPU.
- Shader programs and GPU textures are cached and reused.
- Explicit `free()`/remaining-use counts return texture storage to the pool.
- A tensor only crosses back to JavaScript when code calls `get()`.

This is why Bellsack can perform millions of scalar-field evaluations while remaining a browser application.

## Default frame loop

The browser frame coordinator:

1. Measures and clamps elapsed time.
2. Reads keyboard, mouse, and gamepad state.
3. Resolves raw inputs into Var-backed game actions.
4. Applies camera and editor actions.
5. Runs physics and Var integration.
6. Builds and runs the graphics passes.
7. Adds balls, editor overlays, labels, and debugging graphics.
8. Displays the final GPU tensor directly on the WebGL canvas.
9. Schedules the next animation frame.

The default path is `lamglLoopBodyB`. The older `lamglLoopBodyA` remains available for comparison and older experiments.

## Loop B physics

The normal sparse physics route is:

1. Select the nearest 448 balls.
2. Morton-sort them spatially and divide them into 14 groups of 32.
3. Find an enclosing sphere for each group.
4. Give each group only terrain waves whose bounding spheres could touch one of its balls.
5. Pack that local terrain into a GPU texture row.
6. Run multiple nearest-surface searches per ball in parallel.
7. Merge the candidates, retaining the best approximate surface point.
8. Sample signed distance in the neutral state and under small perturbations of relevant terrain coordinates and ball X/Y/Z.
9. Pack four signed-distance scalars per texel and read that smaller result to the CPU.
10. Convert finite differences into a contact Jacobian and apply sequential impulses.
11. Perform ball-ball response and gravity.
12. Integrate the affected Vars.

The nearest-surface search is a Newton-like iteration. It repeatedly samples density and a tetrahedral finite-difference gradient, then moves approximately by:

```text
point -= gradient * density / |gradient|² * speed
```

An additional term can favor a surface whose normal points toward the ball. Multiprobe starts help avoid saddle points and local minima. The default full multiprobe path currently has 17 starting positions per ball; an optional cached two-probe path also exists.

For deformable terrain contact, Bellsack estimates:

```text
Jᵢ = change in signed distance / change in Var i
```

It then computes an impulse across the ball and terrain coordinates together. Consequently, collision momentum can alter both the ball and the terrain wave parameters.

## Graphics

Loop B uses sparse raymarching:

- The view is divided into four depth bands.
- Current grids are 2×2, 2×2, 4×4, and 8×8: 88 spatial rows across four full-image GPU passes.
- Conservative frustum/bounding-sphere tests assign only relevant waves to each row.
- Each pixel selects the appropriate terrain row and marches along its camera ray looking for a density-zero crossing.
- Successive depth passes retain the previous closest hit.
- The hits are converted into an RGB-plus-depth tensor.
- A separate pass composites ordinary balls.
- Optional CPU-generated editor rings and lines are uploaded and merged.
- The final tensor is displayed without a full-image CPU readback unless a screenshot or diagnostic explicitly requests one.

## Editing and controls

Input state and control bindings live in Varjs rather than a parallel configuration object. Multiple physical controls may map to the same tool.

Existing tools include:

- moving and turning the camera
- shooting or dropping balls
- selecting and unselecting Vars
- moving or resizing waves
- manipulating parameter handles and joints
- adding or deleting waves
- editing species
- copying and pasting selections
- choosing quicksave slots

The editor exposes the shape parameters as colored 3D handles. “Spider” joints can make parameters of different waves behave as one shared coordinate during integration and collision impulses.

## Saving

Bellsack supports two formats:

- Varjs JSON
- BellDag binary snapshots

BellDag is an immutable SHA-256-addressed binary DAG. BellDog bridges that immutable representation to the mutable Var tree.

State can be:

- quicksaved to browser `localStorage` in slots 1–9
- copied through the main text box
- saved to a file
- loaded from a file

Runtime-only `UI` and `Phy` branches under balls and waves are normally excluded, then reconstructed after loading.

## Experimental multiplayer

The HTML embeds a small Tomcat JSP relay and a browser-side BellDag streaming client.

The current model is:

- The first browser becomes the room’s master.
- The master runs physics and periodically broadcasts world snapshots.
- Clients disable their own physics, apply those snapshots, and send compact shooting events to the master.
- Each client retains its own `q.User` subtree, including camera and controls.

It is explicitly an early relay experiment: it has no authentication, TLS, durable world storage, or validation of inner BellDag hashes.

## Current character of the project

Bellsack is presently both an engine and an active numerical-physics laboratory. The functional core is already substantial, but several surrounding systems remain experimental:

- nearest-isosurface reliability is still being refined
- Loop B is replacing Loop A
- player-authored species and the editor are evolving
- VarUI is incomplete
- Sak is only partly implemented
- the embedded starter-game resource is still a placeholder
- multiplayer is a basic master/client experiment
- some authoritative state still lives in `BSx` while being migrated into Varjs

The whole implementation is self-contained in [Bellsack06XX.html](J:/q/Q63x/w/bellsack/codex06XX/Bellsack06XX.html), and I made no changes while producing this summary.

> Is multi mode shader the FIRST shader to be compiled?

Yes—with one literal nuance.

The first compiled WebGL program is the multi-mode program. Inside that program Lamgl performs:

1. Compile its small vertex shader.
2. Compile the multi-mode fragment shader.
3. Link and validate the pair.
4. Compile the other programs afterward.

So the multi-mode fragment shader is technically the second shader object compiled, because its paired vertex shader comes first. But it belongs to the **first program compiled**, and that first program consumes nearly all the initial compilation time.

In one measured run:

- Multi-mode vertex shader finished at `...336.0952`
- Multi-mode fragment shader finished at `...336.1039`
- Multi-mode program linked at `...337.6617`
- The next program finished at `...337.6645`

Therefore no other Bellsack program compiles before the multi-mode program.

> are you using screen coords or canvas coords? cuz that canvas is highly magnified

<details><summary>1 previous message</summary>

> I’ll trace the mouse conversion and projection dimensions directly. The important question is whether both are expressed in CSS/display pixels or whether one side uses the low-resolution backing canvas.
</details>

There is a coordinate-unit mismatch.

- Mouse picking uses CSS/screen pixels: `clientX/clientY` relative to `getBoundingClientRect()`.
- Ring projection also uses the canvas’s displayed CSS width and height.
- Therefore `WaveRingGrabPixelsThick = 10` currently means 10 CSS pixels.
- But `WaveRingDisplayPixelsThick = 2` is applied to the low-resolution backing image before the canvas is magnified.

So if the canvas is magnified 8×, a 2-pixel rendered ring appears roughly 16 CSS pixels thick, while its grab distance is only 10 CSS pixels—not five times wider.

That likely explains what you’re seeing. The correct fix is to put displayed thickness and selectable thickness into the same coordinate system, accounting for canvas magnification. I have not changed anything yet.

- Selected only: original hue pulses brighter/darker.
- Mouse-over only: steady complementary hue.
- Both on the same ring/line: complementary hue pulses brighter/darker.

> Yes. **That is the next mod I’d do.** Keep `densityAtXYZI` and summed density machinery essentially untouched, and replace the current branchy multimode state machine with a straight arithmetic controller.
>
> I would make one adjustment to your history idea:
>
> **Do not store the last 10 query `vec4`s unless a mode actually needs arbitrary old positions. Store only the density floats. Reconstruct positions from state + known offsets.**
>
> For Newton, the ten query positions are deterministic offsets from the current Newton position, so keeping ten `vec4`s wastes 40 floats of live state when you only need ten results.
>
> Something conceptually like:
>
> ```glsl
> // Mode weights, exactly one is 1.
> // Better as already-one-hot float uniforms if practical.
> float mn;
> float mp;
> float mr;
>
> // States for all three modes.
> vec4 nState;
> vec4 pState;
> vec4 rState;
>
> // density history
> float d0,d1,d2,d3,d4,d5,d6,d7,d8,d9;
>
> for(int k=0; k<workLimit; k++){
>
>     // All three modes calculate their candidate query every iteration.
>     vec4 qN = ...;
>     vec4 qP = ...;
>     vec4 qR = ...;
>
>     // No branch selecting a mode.
>     vec4 q =
>         mn*qN +
>         mp*qP +
>         mr*qR;
>
>     float d = densityAtXYZI(q); // ONLY CALL SITE
>
>     // Shift density history.
>     d9=d8;
>     d8=d7;
>     d7=d6;
>     d6=d5;
>     d5=d4;
>     d4=d3;
>     d3=d2;
>     d2=d1;
>     d1=d0;
>     d0=d;
>
>     // Compute ALL mode state updates.
>     nState = ...;
>     pState = ...;
>     rState = ...;
> }
> ```
>
> But given what Firefox did to your large dynamically indexed scalar arrays, I would **not initially write**:
>
> ```glsl
> float d[10];
>
> for(int i=9;i>0;i--)
>     d[i]=d[i-1];
> ```
>
> That's inviting ANGLE to perform another interpretive dance involving robust array indexing.
>
> Start with either explicitly named scalars:
>
> ```glsl
> float d0,d1,d2,d3,d4,d5,d6,d7,d8,d9;
> ```
>
> or, probably even nicer, **three vec4 registers containing 12 density results**:
>
> ```glsl
> vec4 dh0;
> vec4 dh1;
> vec4 dh2;
> ```
>
> You can shift them with fixed swizzles/constructions. That gives the compiler fixed vector accesses and no dynamic private-array indexing.
>
> For example, oldest/newest convention aside:
>
> ```glsl
> dh2 = vec4(dh1.w, dh2.xyz);
> dh1 = vec4(dh0.w, dh1.xyz);
> dh0 = vec4(d, dh0.xyz);
> ```
>
> That's only three assignments to retain twelve density results. Much cleaner than ten scalar stores.
>
> ### Newton
>
> Newton can use:
>
> ```text
> last 10 densities
> -
> current Newton xyz
> -
> the known 10 fixed offset definitions
> ```
>
> No stored sample XYZs required.
>
> Your proposed 4-bit offset encoding in `I` may make even the query generation tiny:
>
> ```glsl
> qN = vec4(newtonXYZ, baseI + offsetId);
> ```
>
> if `densityAtXYZI` interprets those low bits as the predefined XYZ perturbation.
>
> Then Newton doesn't even construct ten different tetrahedral offsets outside density.
>
> ### Perturb
>
> Probably only needs its last ~3 density results, so it can read the newest components of the same history:
>
> ```text
> d0 d1 d2
> ```
>
> and ignore the rest.
>
> ### Ray
>
> Ray generally needs previous/current density, plus its own scalar ray state:
>
> ```text
> t
> previousT
> loT
> hiT
> etc.
> ```
>
> It should not need ten old query vec4s either. Reconstruct XYZ from:
>
> ```glsl
> rayStart + rayDirection*t
> ```
>
> So again density history is enough.
>
> ### Important structural goal
>
> I'd make the code literally resemble:
>
> ```text
> calculate Newton proposed query
> calculate Perturb proposed query
> calculate Ray proposed query
>
> multiply/add the 3 queries into ONE query
>
>              ↓
>
>         densityAtXYZI
>         ONE CALL SITE
>
>              ↓
>
> shift density history
>
> calculate Newton next state
> calculate Perturb next state
> calculate Ray next state
>
> repeat
> ```
>
> No:
>
> ```glsl
> if(mode...)
> switch(mode...)
> ?:
> break
> continue
> ```
>
> in that controller.
>
> And ideally no mode comparisons either. Instead of:
>
> ```glsl
> float mn = mode==0 ? 1. : 0.;
> ```
>
> have JS provide directly:
>
> ```glsl
> uniform float ModeNewton;
> uniform float ModePerturb;
> uniform float ModeRay;
> ```
>
> as one-hot `0/1` values.
>
> Then:
>
> ```glsl
> q = ModeNewton*qN
>   + ModePerturb*qP
>   + ModeRay*qR;
> ```
>
> The compiler doesn't even have to prove that some integer comparison is uniform.
>
> One unavoidable distinction: **the loop itself still has a loop backedge/termination test**, because with one syntactic `densityAtXYZI` callsite that's how you execute it many times. What we're eliminating is all the **algorithm/mode/state branching between density evaluations**.
>
> I think **3 `vec4`s of density history rather than `float[10]`** is the version I'd try first. It matches the same lesson that pushed the big wave cache toward `vec4`: give ANGLE fixed vector operations rather than interesting scalar-array indexing and hope it refrains from inventing 80,000 characters of translated shader in response.

> Why is it that Wave[4] is in gelerated glsl?

<details><summary>1 previous message</summary>

> I won’t change code. I’ll trace the current density layout and generated GLSL around `Wave[4]`, then propose a bulk connection UI that uses your `(Var, number)` point model instead of relying on visually ambiguous dragging.

`Wave[4]` is the wave’s own `.p`, used as its weight.

The packed layout is:

```text
Wave[0] = wave.X.p
Wave[1] = wave.Y.p
Wave[2] = wave.Z.p
Wave[3] = wave.R.p
Wave[4] = wave.p          // weight
Wave[5...] = species-specific parameters
```

The layout deliberately starts with `['X','Y','Z','R','']`; the empty name means “use the wave Var itself.” The generated density code then does approximately:

```text
density += insideBoundingSphere * Wave[4] * speciesFunction(...)
```

That is visible in [Bellsack06XXgptFreeEdit.html](J:/q/Q63x/w/bellsack/codex06XX/Bellsack06XXgptFreeEdit.html:13292).

So the wave is not literally its own child. It occupies a scalar slot alongside its children because every species needs a standard per-wave influence/weight. Currently `wave.p` also participates in deciding whether a wave is active, although conceptually weight and liveness may eventually deserve separate Vars.

There is another unrelated “4”: shard payload starts at `Vec[4]` because `Vec[0..3]` are reserved scratch/query values. After a record is copied into the local `Wave[]`, its local index 4 is the weight.

## The `(Var, number)` coordinate

I think this is a good canonical address:

```text
SpiderPoint = (Var, t)
```

For a scalar child Var:

```text
t = 0    parent’s hand—the wave center
t = 1    elbow, calculated with eeX(), eeY(), eeZ()
t = 2    hand, stored in absolute game coordinates
```

Between them:

```text
0 <= t <= 1: interpolate parent hand → elbow
1 <= t <= 2: interpolate elbow → hand
```

For a root wave, its hand is `[wave.X.p, wave.Y.p, wave.Z.p]`. It has no separately drawn elbow or arm. A child’s `t=0` therefore equals its wave’s hand.

This gives picking a stable semantic result instead of merely returning an arbitrary `vec3`:

```text
picked Var
picked t
derived world position
```

The world position can always be recalculated as things move. The mouse cursor’s screen/depth coordinates are only used to discover `(Var,t)`.

I would keep the tool action separate from the picked coordinate. For example, picking `(Frequency,1.63)` precisely identifies where the user clicked, but:

- Move-wave mode manipulates the parent wave.
- Move-elbow mode manipulates the elbow.
- Move-joint mode manipulates the hand/joint.
- Select mode merely selects the Var.

Otherwise dragging a continuous intermediate `t` becomes mathematically awkward: moving an endpoint affects the grabbed point by only part of the endpoint’s movement.

## Bulk joining: use a connection workbench

I would stop making drag-and-drop the primary way to form joints. Keep 3D clicking for choosing things, but make joining a discrete, transactional operation.

The workbench would have two selection trays:

```text
SOURCE SET                         TARGET SET
wave7.Frequency                    wave12.Frequency
wave7.Width                        wave12.Width
wave8.Frequency                    wave13.Frequency
...
```

Vars can be added through:

- Clicking in 3D.
- Shift-clicking ranges in the Var editor.
- Lassoing visible arms.
- Selecting all arms of chosen waves.
- Filtering by species or field name.
- “Same field on selected waves.”

Then provide a small set of exact operations:

- **Join all into one joint**
- **Pair by row**
- **Pair by field name**
- **Join every source to one target**
- **Join nearest compatible pairs**
- **Detach selected**
- **Detach entire joint**
- **Split selected members into a new joint**

Before applying, show a preview such as:

```text
12 Vars selected
6 joints will be merged into 3
2 incompatible X/Y/Z types skipped
0 ambiguous matches
```

Apply the whole operation atomically, with one Undo.

## Important limitation of the current joint model

Current Edjoints are equivalence groups: compatible Vars with the same immutable key belong to one joint. Therefore joining A–B and B–C also means A–C. They are all aliases in one group.

That means an arbitrary checkbox adjacency matrix would be misleading: you cannot currently express:

```text
A connected to B
B connected to C
A not connected to C
```

For the current model, the UI should emphasize colored **joint groups**, not independent pairwise edges. If you eventually want arbitrary pairwise springs or constraints, that should be a separate connection/link object rather than overloading Edjoint identity.

## Making dense scenes understandable

When the workbench is open, the 3D view should enter a focus mode:

- Selected source Vars use one brightness pulse.
- Selected targets use another frequency.
- Existing members of the relevant joints remain bright.
- Everything unrelated becomes faint or hidden.
- Each joint gets a short label and member count.
- Preview connections are drawn differently from committed ones.
- A “show only selected waves/joints” toggle removes the forest of unrelated arms.

That solves both possibilities you mentioned: buggy dragging and dragging that works but is visually lost among hundreds of Eds.

My preferred workflow would be: select waves, choose “matching fields,” preview the generated joint groups, then apply once. Dragging can remain as a fine-adjustment tool, but large-scale topology editing should not depend on pixel-perfect dragging.

> how does my proposal differ from existing drag behavior

<details><summary>1 previous message</summary>

> I’ll compare your `(Var,t)` proposal against the exact values the current picker and drag state retain, especially what happens when the mouse lands on the center–elbow segment versus the elbow–hand segment. No code changes.
</details>

Your proposal mostly changes the representation of a picked location, but it could also imply a larger topology change depending on whether joining is allowed at every `t`.

| Concept | Existing behavior | Your `(Var,t)` proposal |
|---|---|---|
| Parent/center | `{kind:"waveCenter", point:vec3}` or inferred from an Ed line | `(childVar,0)` |
| Elbow | `{kind:"edAnchor", edVar, point:vec3}` | `(var,1)` using `eeX/Y/Z()` |
| Hand | `{kind:"edTip", edVar, point:vec3}` | `(var,2)` using absolute hand coordinates |
| Line interior | `{kind:"edLine", edVar, point:vec3}` | Continuous `t`: `0..1` or `1..2` |
| Persistent identity | Kind plus a temporary world-space point | One Var plus one scalar |
| Which segment was clicked | Lost—both segments become `edLine` | Encoded by whether `t<1` or `t>1` |

The important difference is that the current picker calculates the correct perspective-adjusted 3D point on either line segment, but then throws away its parameter and segment identity. Both become merely:

```text
{ edVar, kind:"edLine", point:[x,y,z] }
```

Your proposal retains that information:

```text
(var, 0.37)   // center-to-elbow segment
(var, 1.64)   // elbow-to-hand segment
```

## Current mouse dragging is more surprising than your model

For mouse dragging, Bellsack currently normalizes:

```text
elbow       → edLine
first line  → edLine
second line → edLine
hand        → edTip
```

Then every mouse Ed drag sets `mouseEhOnly=true`. Consequently:

- Starting on the hand moves the entire coincident hand/joint bundle.
- Starting on an elbow or either segment moves only that Var’s **hand**.
- It does not move the elbow, even when you clicked directly on the elbow.
- The clicked world point is used to calculate drag delta, but the thing changed is still `eh`.
- Dropping anywhere on another Ed—center-to-elbow segment, elbow, elbow-to-hand segment, or hand—snaps to that target Var’s **hand**.
- If released without a snap target, the hand is restored.

That explains why dragging may look broken: you can click an elbow or a line and see a different endpoint—the hand—move, potentially underneath many other lines.

Gamepad/cursor3d behavior is different: it preserves more of the original `kind`, so an `edAnchor` can move the elbow. Mouse behavior deliberately converts that into hand movement.

## What your proposal does not specify yet

A `(Var,t)` tells Bellsack exactly where you grabbed, but not necessarily what dragging that point should modify.

There are two possible meanings:

1. **Picking-coordinate only**

   `(Var,t)` identifies the clicked position, but the selected tool decides what moves.

   - Move elbow tool changes `ee`.
   - Move joint tool changes `eh`.
   - Move wave tool changes the parent center.
   - Join always joins hands.

   This is the smallest change and removes the current ambiguity.

2. **Every `t` is a connectable point**

   Dropping onto `(targetVar,0.46)` would create a connection to the interior of its center–elbow segment.

   That is a much larger change. Existing Edjoints join hands by giving Vars equal hand keys. They cannot represent attachment to a moving segment interior without storing the target `(Var,t)` as an actual constraint.

I recommend the first interpretation initially: make `(Var,t)` the universal precise hit/grab address, but keep Edjoint joining hand-to-hand. Then the UI can clearly show:

```text
grabbed Frequency at t=0.46
operation: move Frequency hand
join target: Width hand at t=2
```

That would expose the current behavior instead of silently converting everything into “move the hand.”

> shift-clicking. no i want it to work with mouse by itself

Right—no Shift, keyboard modifiers, or list management. It should be completely usable with the mouse in the 3D view.

I’d use three clickable toolbar modes:

```text
Move | Connect | Disconnect
```

Then all editing uses the left mouse button.

### Connect mode

1. Mouse-down on any part of an Ed, producing `(sourceVar, sourceT)`.
2. Its hand and entire existing joint become brightly highlighted.
3. Keep holding and sweep the mouse across other Eds.
4. Every crossed Ed is added to the preview connection group.
5. Release once to join all collected Vars atomically.

The swept targets could be elbows, hands, or line interiors, but each target is identified precisely as `(Var,t)`. The actual Edjoint operation would still join that Var’s hand unless you decide that interior attachments should become real constraints.

After releasing, the source joint could remain “loaded,” allowing ordinary single clicks to add more Vars without restarting the gesture. Clicking empty space unloads it.

### Disconnect mode

Mouse-down and sweep across Eds. Every crossed Var is previewed as detached. Release once to give each collected Var its own distinct hand key while leaving the hand visually at the same position.

Because current Edjoints are equivalence groups, “disconnect this Var” is precise. “Disconnect only A from B but keep A joined to C when B and C share the same joint” is not representable without changing the topology model.

### Accuracy in crowded scenes

While the mouse is held:

- Dim all Eds except the source joint and possible targets.
- Draw a conspicuous dot at the exact `(Var,t)` under the cursor.
- Show the Var name beside it.
- Prefer the frontmost rendered Ed.
- Use the mouse wheel to cycle through overlapping candidates without moving the pointer.
- Make the collection brush wider than the rendered line.
- Allow dragging a loop around an area to collect all front-visible Eds inside it.
- Double-clicking a wave center could collect all of that wave’s arms.

This makes bulk connection feel like painting topology rather than dragging tiny endpoints together.

The crucial difference from existing dragging is that nothing moves spatially in Connect/Disconnect mode. Mouse movement only collects `(Var,t)` targets and previews a topology transaction. That removes the current confusion where clicking an elbow or line silently starts moving its hand.

> i dont think i wanna handle MOVE anymore by mouse. Theres a set of hands and a set of edjoints. This is simply a mapping hand->ej

Yes. That is much simpler than the interaction I was describing.

The topology is:

```text
Hands H
Edjoints J
jointOf: H → J
```

A hand is identified by its Var. The inverse mapping gives the membership of an Edjoint:

```text
members(ej) = all hands h where jointOf(h) == ej
```

There are no pairwise links and no mouse movement operation. The mouse only changes `jointOf`.

## Mouse operations

Three toolbar tools are sufficient:

- **Join**: mouse-down on a hand chooses its Edjoint as the destination. Sweep/click other hands to assign them to that same Edjoint.
- **Split**: collect several hands and assign all of them to one newly created Edjoint.
- **Separate**: every touched hand gets its own new singleton Edjoint.

All three can preview changes and commit on mouse release.

This handles important cases cleanly:

```text
Join B into A:
jointOf(B) = jointOf(A)

Move several hands from old groups into one existing group:
for each selected hand:
    jointOf(hand) = destinationEj

Split a subset but keep that subset connected:
newEj = createEdjoint()
for each selected hand:
    jointOf(hand) = newEj

Completely disconnect several hands:
for each selected hand:
    jointOf(hand) = createEdjoint()
```

An Edjoint with no remaining hands can disappear.

## Role of `(Var,t)`

`(Var,t)` is only the mouse hit coordinate:

```text
t=0    parent
t=1    elbow
t=2    hand
```

Clicking anywhere along an arm identifies that arm’s hand Var. The exact `t` determines the highlighted point and which overlapping geometry was hit, but it does not move anything and does not become part of the topology.

Thus:

```text
(Width, 0.3)
(Width, 1)
(Width, 1.8)
(Width, 2)
```

all identify the same `Width` hand for mapping purposes.

Clicking the wave itself identifies the wave’s own hand, whose displayed position is the wave center.

## One data-model question remains

The cleanest model is for the Edjoint to own the shared absolute endpoint position:

```text
edjoint.position
jointOf(hand)
```

Then every arm mapped to that Edjoint draws its endpoint at `edjoint.position`. Hand identity belongs to the Var, while endpoint position belongs to the Edjoint.

That is cleaner than the current representation, where joint identity is inferred from equal `(ehX,ehY,ehZ,ei)` values stored in every Var. Explicit `hand → ej` mapping means:

- Identity no longer depends on floating-point coordinate equality.
- Edjoint membership can change without pretending that coordinates define identity.
- Bulk reassignment is straightforward.
- One Edjoint position is not redundantly stored in every member.
- The UI can display and select an actual Edjoint as an object.

So the mouse is not dragging geometry at all. It is painting/reassigning a function from hands to Edjoints.

> If we jsut randomly assigned ej strings to all vars, that would work except for theres a security requirement about waveItselfExistence. its gotta be addable and removable without duplicsation

Exactly.

Ordinary Vars may use random Edjoint strings.

Wave existence needs a reserved canonical key:

```text
wave.eh = wave.nath()
```

Rules:

- Exactly one authoritative wave exists at that nath.
- Adding it twice is idempotent, not duplication.
- Other hands may reference its nath, but cannot create another wave.
- Removing it targets that same canonical identity.

Is removal a tombstone, rather than deleting the Var?

> Lets say a waveEdjointKey is the hash of its nath. with some prefix i guess. Ej$...thenath... makes a .big and u get .name that is its short form

Yes:

```text
waveEdjoint.big  = "Ej$" + wave.nath()
waveEdjoint.name = hash(waveEdjoint.big) // short canonical key
wave.eh          = waveEdjoint.name
```

Same nath always produces the same key:

- Add is idempotent.
- Duplication is impossible.
- Receivers verify `.name` from `.big`.
- The full nath remains recoverable from `.big`.

Loose Edjoints could use a random nonce in `.big`.

> but added to that we gotta know if its X_ Y_ Z_ L_

Put the type inside both the content and short key:

```text
.big  = "Ej$L$" + wave.nath()
.name = "L_" + hash(.big)
```

Likewise:

```text
X_<hash>
Y_<hash>
Z_<hash>
L_<hash>
```

Then `Var.eh` alone contains:

- Edjoint identity
- Edjoint type

Wave existence uses the deterministic `L_` key derived from its nath.

> i think we need more ei types. duplicate most or all of them for waveItself vs nonwaveitself

Yes. Use two type namespaces:

```text
X_  Y_  Z_  L_        ordinary Edjoints

WX_ WY_ WZ_ WR_ WE_   canonical wave Edjoints
```

Where:

```text
WX = wave.X
WY = wave.Y
WZ = wave.Z
WR = wave.R
WE = wave existence / wave.p
```

Each `W*` key is deterministically hashed from the wave nath.

`ei` can be derived from the prefix as an optimization, never primary state.


Mapping:

```text
Cx = wave.X
Cy = wave.Y
Cz = wave.Z
Cr = wave.R
Ce = wave.p / existence
```

Each `C*` key is deterministically derived from the wave nath.

> can a file url loaded html read from a localhost url

Yes, if localhost JSP allows CORS.

A `file://` page usually sends origin `null`. JSP should return:

```http
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *
Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, POST, OPTIONS
Access-Control-Allow-Headers: Content-Type
```

Binary POST causes an `OPTIONS` preflight, which JSP must handle. Chrome may also require private-network preflight headers. Serving `index.html` from the same localhost webapp avoids all of this.

> i want to minimize the round trip time codex->html->codex->html->codex... Is the design I proposed the lowest round trip time for that?

Not quite. Fastest practical design is:

1. Codex atomically writes `in.txt` with a command ID.
2. Browser holds a long-poll request open; JSP responds immediately when `in.txt` changes.
3. Browser evaluates it and POSTs `out.txt` with the same ID.
4. Codex waits using a filesystem watcher, not repeated polling.

This removes polling delays. WebSockets could be slightly faster, but add complexity for negligible localhost benefit. The browser’s shader compilation/rendering will dominate the round trip.

> [Codex waits using a filesystem watcher, not repeated polling.]
> You can do the whole thing event based?

Yes.

- JSP watches `in.txt` and holds the browser’s request open.
- Codex writes a command atomically.
- Browser receives it immediately, evaluates it, then POSTs `out.txt`.
- Codex waits on `FileSystemWatcher` for the matching output ID.

No timed polling is needed. Each command/result uses an ID to avoid stale or missed events.

> i basically want codex to be able to call a js function BS.evalJsCodeFromCodex(string) which returns a string to send back to codex. codex does it whenever codex wants

Yes. The transport can expose exactly that abstraction:

```text
Codex sends: {id, code}
Browser calls: BS.evalJsCodeFromCodex(code)
Browser returns: {id, resultString}
Codex receives resultString
```

It stays synchronous inside Bellsack. The file/JSP event bridge is hidden underneath. Exceptions return their stack as the result. The page only needs to remain open.

> use the time as the id. as float64.
>
> can codex call the network?

Use Unix time as a float64 ID. Only one command will be pending, preventing timestamp collisions.

Codex cannot reliably call localhost directly in this sandbox. But it can write `in.txt` and wait for `out.txt`; the browser performs the network requests to JSP. That path is also faster and more reliable here.

> how does codex get the response

Through the same blocking HTTP request:

1. Codex POSTs `{timeId, code}` to JSP.
2. JSP holds that request open.
3. Browser’s long-poll receives the code.
4. Browser calls `BS.evalJsCodeFromCodex(code)`.
5. Browser POSTs the returned string.
6. JSP completes Codex’s original request with that string.

So one Codex HTTP call directly returns the JavaScript result—fully event-driven, no polling.

> waits... I dont want it waiting. I want low lag. You said you could do it only by events

“Waits” means blocked on a network event—not polling or sleeping.

The BAT’s HTTP call remains open. The instant the browser returns the string, the socket wakes and Codex receives it. That is event-driven and adds essentially no artificial delay.

A direct return necessarily waits for the function to finish.

> how big a content can you put in the params of a bat file

Windows BAT arguments are limited to about 8,191 characters by `cmd.exe`. Quoting and escaping reduce usable space.

`CreateProcess` itself allows roughly 32,767 characters, but BAT files still hit the smaller limit.

Use stdin instead—it streams essentially unlimited JavaScript without argument escaping.

> can you make the jsp only visible on localhost even if i have a public url

Yes. JSP will inspect the actual socket address:

```java
request.getRemoteAddr()
```

It will return `403` unless that address is IPv4 or IPv6 loopback. It will not trust `Host` or `X-Forwarded-For`.

For strongest protection, Tomcat’s Connector should also bind to `127.0.0.1`. A reverse proxy could otherwise make public requests appear local, so it must exclude this JSP.

- `document`: normal browser navigation loaded the HTML. No Bellsack code initiated it.

That confirms it is not Bellsack-specific.

Chrome is producing the warning for unrelated local HTML files. It’s a browser/extension first-load behavior involving `file:` opaque origins—not an application error.

Do not capture it in Bellsack’s errors list. Using localhost instead of `file:` should eliminate it.

> why would it be displayed in network tab

The Network tab tracks URL loads, not only internet traffic.

Chrome loads `file:` documents through its URL-loading machinery, so the initial disk read appears there. If the row’s type is `document` and initiator is `Other`, it came from browser navigation—not page JavaScript. The console warning is about origin access during that load.

> why does chrome say it is an error. did i do something wrong

No, you did nothing wrong.

Chrome labels it an error because it blocked an attempted interaction between two `file:` browsing contexts. Each `file:` page gets a unique opaque security origin—even for the identical path.

Opening the HTML normally is valid. The blocked attempt was likely browser/extension tab handling and is harmless unless something visibly fails. Serving through localhost avoids it.

> its not 2 file browsing contexts

Correct—there aren’t necessarily two visible browsing contexts.

Chrome’s wording is misleading. One tab can contain an old/provisional document and a newly loaded document, each with different opaque `file:` origin tokens. It calls the top-level document a “frame.”

So the message does not prove you opened two pages or created an iframe.

> is it a browser plugin

Possibly, but not proven.

Test the same file in Chrome Guest mode or Incognito with extensions disabled:

- Warning disappears → browser extension/plugin.
- Warning remains → Chrome’s own `file:` navigation behavior.

Given it happens on unrelated HTML files only on first load, an extension is plausible.

This GL error means Lamgl activated more framebuffer outputs than the fragment shader provides. The `256` means the same invalid draw repeated 256 times. It’s a real output-count/state bug, not shader compilation timing.

> it changed in

Found it.

Copy 6 added `rayCameraPointInputPass`. Its fragment shader does not declare:

```glsl
in vec2 uv;
```

So Lamgl mistakes the unmatched vertex-shader `out vec2 uv` for a second texture output. It activates two draw buffers, while the fragment shader outputs only `outColor`. That exactly causes the error 256 times.

The proper fix is making `GLVar.isOutTex()` accept only fragment-shader outputs:

```js
return this.memType === 'out' && this.shaderType === 'sf';
```

> You seem able to run alot of commands on commandline faster than you message to/from JsEval.jsp

Yes.

Command-line calls run directly and usually finish in ~0.3 seconds.

JsEval adds:

- Tomcat HTTP routing
- A browser long-poll cycle
- Browser main-thread availability
- Bellsack’s long GPU/compile frames
- A single-pending-call lock

When Bellsack freezes compiling or a request remains pending, JsEval becomes much slower. Once stable, multiple sequential HTTP calls inside one command should be fairly fast.

> does the whole process require waiting on a timer

No fixed timer is required for normal messages.

The JSP waits, but `notifyAll()` wakes it immediately when a message arrives. Browser XHR callbacks also fire immediately when responses arrive.

Timers are only used for:

- long-poll timeout/reconnect
- failure timeouts
- Bellsack reload/startup
- my deliberate waits during testing

So a healthy round trip should be event-driven.

> i want it to be as fast as possible. bellsack is meant to run at first person shooter gaming-low-lag

The bridge should add essentially zero cost to gameplay while idle.

For lowest latency:

- Keep one browser GET continuously waiting.
- Wake it with `notifyAll()` immediately.
- POST responses immediately.
- No polling interval or retry timer during success.
- Separate the two message directions so one cannot block the other.
- Replace stale pending calls instead of waiting ten minutes.
- Avoid console logging during normal operation.

The remaining delay is browser main-thread blocking during GLSL compilation. Networking cannot interrupt that.

> what happens if i click a webpage and it redirects me to localhost:8080/Bellsack/JsEval.jsp?{thepayload}

<details><summary>2 previous messages</summary>

> Searched the web for `site:developer.mozilla.org same-origin policy cross-origin writes links redirects allowed localhost navigation ...`
>

</details>

That is currently dangerous.

The redirect would:

1. Send the GET request to your local Tomcat.
2. Pass the JSP’s localhost check—the TCP connection comes from your browser at `127.0.0.1`/`::1`.
3. Queue `{thepayload}` as JavaScript.
4. A running Bellsack tab receives and evaluates it.
5. That code could call `BS.codex(...)`, alter Bellsack, or access anything exposed to Bellsack JavaScript.

Same-origin policy does not prevent links or redirects to localhost; cross-origin navigation is generally allowed. The attacker may not read the response, but they do not need to. [MDN](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Security/Defenses/Same-origin_policy), [Chrome PNA notes](https://developer.chrome.com/blog/private-network-access-update)

Therefore, “request came from localhost” is not authentication. We should remove GET execution and require an unguessable session token for every POST.

> propose only stateless ways

Stateless options, strongest first:

1. Signed POSTs

- Codex signs `timestamp + payload` with Ed25519.
- JSP stores only Codex’s public key.
- JSP verifies every request.
- Reject timestamps outside perhaps 10 seconds.
- No GET execution.

2. Shared-secret HMAC

- JSP and Codex share a random 256-bit secret.
- POST contains `timestamp`, payload, and HMAC.
- JSP verifies without storing sessions.

3. Random capability

- Require a long random value in every POST body.
- Simpler, but weaker than signing.

Add stateless browser checks to all options:

- Reject `GET`.
- Reject `Sec-Fetch-Mode: navigate`.
- Reject `Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site`.
- Remove `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`.

No stateless design can completely prevent replay of a captured valid request; timestamps only limit its lifetime. I prefer signed POSTs.

> how can i make it so it only accepts network requests from that browsr tab

The server cannot identify a browser tab from IP, cookies, Origin, or headers. Cookies are shared between tabs.

Practical solution:

1. Launcher generates a random 256-bit per-tab secret.
2. Pass it in the Bellsack URL fragment:

```text
Bellsack06XX.html#jsEvalKey=...
```

Fragments are not sent in HTTP requests.

3. Bellsack reads it once, removes it from the address bar, and keeps it inside a private closure.
4. Every JsEval POST includes an HMAC made with that secret.
5. JSP receives the same secret from the launcher and verifies each request statelessly.

Other webpages and tabs cannot produce the HMAC. A redirect to `JsEval.jsp?payload` fails.

Limitation: arbitrary JavaScript already executing inside the authorized Bellsack tab could call its authorized bridge. Preventing that requires a browser extension with a per-tab isolated secret.

> what if i ed25519 sign each message and generate it from a password, as in the user/pass part of left panel

Yes. That can be stateless and secure enough for this local bridge.

Design:

- Derive a 32-byte Ed25519 seed from `username + password` using Argon2id—not a plain hash. [RFC 9106](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9106/)
- Keep the private key inside that Bellsack tab.
- JSP contains the expected public key.
- POST each payload with timestamp and signature over:

```text
"Bellsack JsEval v1" + username + timestamp + payload
```

- JSP verifies the signature and rejects old timestamps. Ed25519 uses a 32-byte private seed and 64-byte signatures. [RFC 8032](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc8032/)

Important limitations:

- Any tab knowing the same username/password can sign.
- A captured signed message can be replayed during the timestamp window.
- A weak password can be guessed offline by comparing derived public keys.
- Never let the requester supply an arbitrary public key; JSP must already trust that user’s public key.

Use a separate derived subkey for JsEval rather than using the multiplayer password/key directly.

> is this only a danger for BS.codex/codexx? it seems not a danger for codex -> bellsack -> codex

No. The redirect attacks the opposite direction first:

```text
malicious webpage → JsEval.jsp → Bellsack evaluates payload
```

That impersonates Codex.

The payload can then call:

```text
Bellsack → BS.codex/codexx → Codex
```

So it can attack both directions.

A real Codex → Bellsack → Codex round trip is safe only if:

- Bellsack verifies Codex’s signature on the command.
- Codex verifies Bellsack’s signature on the response.
- The response signs the hash of the original command, binding them together.

> is there something fast and easy i can do to secure this. i dont have ed25519 hooked in yet

Yes. Use a random capability token.

Fastest simple design:

- Generate a random 43-character base62 token.
- Put only its SHA-256 hash in `JsEval.jsp`.
- Enter the raw token in Bellsack’s user/password panel.
- Include it inside every POST body.
- JSP hashes it and uses constant-time comparison.
- Reject every GET request.
- Reject requests with `Sec-Fetch-Mode: navigate`.

This is stateless, requires no Ed25519, and one SHA-256 per message is negligible.

Do not store the raw token in the public Bellsack HTML. Use a separate random token for JsEval.

> what if i type in the codex window  but let codex still do codex->bellsack->codex

That is much safer.

Disable unsolicited:

```text
Bellsack → BS.codex/codexx → Codex
```

Keep only:

```text
You type in Codex
Codex → authenticated POST → Bellsack
Bellsack → result of that same call → Codex
```

Then Bellsack’s return is only a response, never a new command for Codex.

You still need a random token on Codex’s POST; otherwise a malicious webpage can impersonate Codex and inject JavaScript into Bellsack. But you do not need Ed25519 yet—POST-only plus the random capability is enough.

> codex is calling JsEval.jsp for codex->browser right

Yes.

Current path:

```text
Codex → GET/POST JsEval.jsp → waiting Bellsack tab
Bellsack evaluates JavaScript → POSTs result to JsEval.jsp
JsEval.jsp returns that result to Codex
```

That same public GET/POST entry point is why an unrelated webpage can currently impersonate Codex.

> so someone could call the jsp to message the browser to message codex. instead of calling the jsp to message codex. its the same problem

Exactly. It’s the same underlying vulnerability:

```text
attacker → JsEval.jsp → Bellsack → BS.codex → Codex
```

The browser becomes a relay, so disabling only direct JSP-to-Codex messaging is insufficient.

The first hop must be authenticated. `JsEval.jsp` must reject any code-injection request lacking Codex’s random capability token. Then the attacker cannot make Bellsack relay anything.

> what happens if a browser redirects to a localhost url

A redirect performs a top-level GET to localhost.

The local server sees:

```text
remote address = 127.0.0.1 or ::1
```

So the current JSP accepts it as local. CORS generally does not block top-level navigation.

With current JsEval:

- If another Bellsack tab is listening, the query payload is sent there and evaluated.
- The redirected tab waits for and displays the evaluation result.
- If the redirected tab was the only Bellsack tab, it navigates away and no listener remains, so the request eventually times out.

The originating website usually cannot read the response, but it can still trigger the action.

> i only want CORS for BellsackServer*.jsp, not for this codex thing

That’s the correct separation.

`JsEval.jsp` should have no CORS headers. But then a `file://` Bellsack page cannot read its AJAX responses.

Bellsack must instead load from the same origin:

```text
http://localhost:8080/Bellsack/Bellsack06XX.html
```

Also, removing CORS does not block redirects or form submissions. JsEval should still:

- Reject executable GET requests.
- Accept authenticated POST only.
- Require the random capability token.

`BellsackServer*.jsp` can retain its separate CORS policy.

Yes—use the browser password manager, not cookies or HTML storage:

```html
<input name="username" autocomplete="username">
<input name="password" type="password" autocomplete="current-password">
```

Then:

1. Password manager fills it.
2. Bellsack derives the Ed25519 key.
3. Clear the password field.
4. Keep the private key only in that tab’s memory.
5. Store only the public key and KDF salt persistently.

Multiple HTML files served from the same `http://localhost:8080` origin can share password-manager credentials and IndexedDB. `file://` sharing is unreliable because file origins are often opaque. [MDN](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Security/Defenses/Same-origin_policy)

Do not store the raw password/private seed in cookies or `localStorage`. For tab isolation, memory is best; `sessionStorage` is tab-specific but readable by JavaScript. [MDN](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/sessionStorage)

> but it must be there while NOT using bellsack html or else the remember password is useless

The browser password manager persists while Bellsack is closed. It lives in the browser profile, not the HTML.

When any Bellsack HTML opens:

1. Password manager autofills.
2. Bellsack derives the private key.
3. Signing works until that tab closes.

While no Bellsack tab exists, no private key is needed because there is no browser listener. `JsEval.jsp` only keeps the public key.

Serve all versions from the same localhost origin so the saved login applies to all of them.

> what im saying is another html file run locally could get the same password field autofilled

Yes. Any local HTML served from the same origin could imitate the login form and potentially receive the same autofilled password.

Therefore password autofill does not prove “this Bellsack tab.”

Use a dedicated origin for trusted Bellsack pages, such as:

```text
http://bellsack-codex.localhost:8080/
```

Never serve unrelated HTML from that origin. For stronger isolation, use a dedicated browser profile or require manual password-manager selection instead of automatic filling.

> what if i generate the password on server and send it to the html

That is better—if the server also serves the trusted Bellsack HTML and JsEval has no CORS.

Use this flow:

1. Server generates a random per-tab capability.
2. Embed it inside the Bellsack HTML response—not the URL.
3. Bellsack keeps it only in memory.
4. Every bridge request includes it.
5. The server rejects requests without it.

An unrelated webpage can redirect to localhost, but cannot read the returned capability because it is cross-origin.

For a stateless server, make the capability:

```text
expiry + random tab value + server HMAC
```

The JSP verifies the HMAC without remembering the tab.

Limitations:

- Untrusted HTML served from the same localhost origin could obtain its own capability.
- The capability disappears when the tab closes.
- Never expose it through CORS, URLs, logs, or `localStorage`.

Yes. You have three ways to avoid copying the password every time:

- Browser password manager on a dedicated Bellsack origin.
- Generate the Ed25519 key once and store a non-extractable `CryptoKey` in IndexedDB. [MDN](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/SubtleCrypto)
- Use a passkey/WebAuthn with Windows Hello, PIN, fingerprint, or security key. The authenticator stores the private key and verifies user presence. [MDN](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Security/Authentication/Passkeys)

Important: if Bellsack automatically signs every `BS.codex` message, another player who triggers that function could still produce a valid message appearing to be yours. To prove it was personally authorized, show the exact message and require your confirmation before signing.

> Is there any secure password store for a file url

<details><summary>2 previous messages</summary>

> Not reliably across browsers. I’m checking whether WebAuthn or browser credential storage supports `file://` origins safely.
>
> <details><summary>Searched the web</summary>
>
> Searched the web for `site:w3.org WebAuthn file origin rp id file URL prohibited ...`
>
> </details>
</details>

No standardized, reliable secure password store exists for arbitrary `file://` pages.

Problems:

- `file://` pages usually have opaque origins, so storage behavior is browser-dependent. [MDN](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Security/Defenses/Same-origin_policy)
- WebAuthn requires a domain-based relying-party identity, which a file URL lacks. [W3C](https://www.w3.org/TR/webauthn-3/)
- Windows Credential Manager is not directly available to webpage JavaScript.
- IndexedDB/localStorage are not secure secret vaults and may behave inconsistently for file origins.

Practical choices:

- Serve Bellsack from a dedicated `http://bellsack-codex.localhost` origin and use WebAuthn or a non-extractable `CryptoKey`.
- Make a small browser extension that holds the key and signs only for the authorized tab.
- Continue using `file://` and enter/unlock the password each browser session.

The dedicated localhost origin is the easiest robust option.

> what about for locahost or 127.0.0.1 urls

For `localhost` URLs, yes. Browsers treat localhost as a secure context.

Best options:

- Passkey/WebAuthn: strongest. The private key stays in Windows Hello, a password manager, or security key.
- Non-extractable WebCrypto key stored in IndexedDB: persistent, but any JavaScript on the same origin can use it.
- Browser password manager: can remember and autofill the password.
- `HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict` cookie: good for server authentication, but JavaScript cannot use it for Ed25519 signing.

Use a dedicated origin such as:

`http://bellsack-codex.localhost:8080`

Do not mix it with unrelated HTML. `localhost` and `127.0.0.1` are different origins and do not share normal web storage. Prefer the named `.localhost` origin for passkeys and stable identity. [MDN](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Security/Defenses/Secure_Contexts)

> systems that exist in browser

Browser-native systems available on localhost:

- Password manager: remembers and autofills username/password.
- Passkeys/WebAuthn: browser or Windows Hello stores the private key and asks for PIN/biometric confirmation.
- WebCrypto + IndexedDB: stores a non-extractable Ed25519 `CryptoKey`.
- HttpOnly cookies: browser securely stores a server session credential, inaccessible to JavaScript.
- `sessionStorage`: tab-specific, but readable by same-origin JavaScript.
- `localStorage`: persistent, but not appropriate for passwords or private keys.

For your existing Ed25519 design, WebCrypto plus IndexedDB fits best. For strongest user-presence proof, use WebAuthn.

> systems that exist in both chrome and firefox

<details><summary>2 previous messages</summary>

Available in both Chrome and Firefox:

- WebAuthn/passkeys — strongest user-authentication option. Both support the standard API, though their passkey-provider UI differs. [MDN](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Web_Authentication_API)
- WebCrypto Ed25519 — available in current versions of both.
- IndexedDB — both can persist a non-extractable `CryptoKey`.
- Built-in password managers — both remember passwords, but their databases are separate.
- HttpOnly/SameSite cookies — supported by both, but JavaScript cannot use them to sign.
- `localStorage` and `sessionStorage` — supported but unsuitable for private keys/passwords.

For Bellsack, the common approach is WebCrypto Ed25519 plus IndexedDB on a dedicated localhost origin. Chrome and Firefox would each have their own stored key unless you derive/import the same key in both.

> that do not require extra hardware

Without extra hardware, both Chrome and Firefox support:

- WebCrypto Ed25519 key stored as non-extractable in IndexedDB.
- Browser password manager storing the password.
- WebAuthn through Windows Hello using a PIN, if configured.
- HttpOnly cookies for server authentication.

Best fit for Bellsack: generate/store a non-extractable Ed25519 `CryptoKey` in IndexedDB on a dedicated localhost origin. No password copying and no extra hardware. Any JavaScript from that same origin could still request signatures, so keep unrelated HTML off that origin.

> what about a http header, does browser repeat existing headers given to it

A browser does not echo arbitrary response headers. If the server sends `X-Secret: abc`, later requests will not repeat it.

The standard automatic mechanism is a cookie:

`Set-Cookie: BellsackCodex=randomSecret; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict; Path=/Bellsack/JsEval.jsp`

Chrome and Firefox then automatically send it back as a `Cookie` header for matching requests.

Useful properties:

- `HttpOnly`: page JavaScript cannot read it.
- `SameSite=Strict`: cross-site redirects, forms, and iframes should not send it.
- `Path`: limits where it is sent.

It is shared by tabs in that browser profile, so it authenticates the browser session—not one tab or your personal identity. [MDN](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/Cookies)

> can a html file get a http header

A `file://` HTML file has no HTTP response, so it cannot receive HTTP headers when loaded.

Its JavaScript can request an HTTP URL with `fetch`/XHR and read permitted response headers only if that server allows CORS. Custom headers also require `Access-Control-Expose-Headers`.

It cannot read headers from a cross-origin iframe or redirect.

So for browser-managed cookies or headers without CORS, serve Bellsack itself from localhost instead of `file://`.

> i could put it in tomcat

Yes. That is the cleanest solution.

Serve both from:

- `http://localhost:8080/Bellsack/Bellsack06XX.html`
- `http://localhost:8080/Bellsack/JsEval.jsp`

Then they share one origin. You can remove JsEval CORS and use HttpOnly, SameSite cookies or IndexedDB/WebCrypto reliably.

Do not deploy/run `BellsackServer*.jsp` in that setup at the same time. Its source may remain embedded in the HTML; embedded source does not execute.

> what if theres 2 html files on that same tomcat server and i happen to load both of them

Both HTML tabs share the same:

- Cookies
- IndexedDB
- `localStorage`
- Origin permissions
- Stored WebCrypto keys

Both could connect to `JsEval.jsp`. With the current single-listener design, whichever tab’s waiting request arrives first may receive Codex’s command. So commands could reach the wrong Bellsack version.

To distinguish tabs, give each tab a random capability stored only in memory or `sessionStorage`, and have Codex address that capability.

If the two HTML files should not trust each other, serve them from different hostnames, such as:

- `bellsack-a.localhost`
- `bellsack-b.localhost`

Paths alone are not a security boundary.

> are you saying i can prove a network message came from the browser tab that opened a html from the locahost tomcat

You can prove that a message was signed by a private key held by that specific page instance.

Process:

1. The localhost-served HTML generates a new non-extractable keypair in memory.
2. The server records or certifies that tab’s public key.
3. Every message includes a timestamp, payload, and signature.
4. Tomcat or Codex verifies the signature.

That distinguishes two tabs, even when they loaded the same HTML.

It proves “code with access to this tab’s key sent the message.” It does not prove you personally approved it; malicious JavaScript executing inside that same tab could also request a signature. Cookies alone only prove the browser profile, not a specific tab.

> the question is where to store the password (that deterministicly generates the privatekey)

Store it in the browser’s password manager, scoped to a dedicated Bellsack localhost origin.

Better: after the first unlock:

1. Read the autofilled password.
2. Derive the Ed25519 private key.
3. Import it as a non-extractable `CryptoKey`.
4. Save that key in IndexedDB.
5. Clear the password field.

Later, Bellsack loads the key directly; the password is needed only for recovery or another browser.

Do not store the password itself in cookies, IndexedDB, `localStorage`, or `sessionStorage`.

Any HTML on the same origin can use the stored key, so unrelated HTML must use another hostname.

> so if there is only 1 html on localhost

Then WebCrypto plus IndexedDB is reasonable.

That single trusted HTML can retrieve and use the non-extractable private key without storing the password.

Remaining risk: JavaScript injected into that HTML—such as through unsecured JsEval.jsp—could use the key to sign messages even though it cannot extract it. So authenticate Codex-to-browser messages before evaluating them, or require your confirmation before signing outgoing Codex messages.

> i am looking for a place to read and write a string value where others wont see it

If your HTML JavaScript can read a secret string, any malicious JavaScript running in that same page/origin can also read it. Browsers provide no protected plaintext-string vault for page JavaScript.

Choices:

- Hide from other origins: IndexedDB on a dedicated origin.
- Hide from all JavaScript: HttpOnly cookie, but only Tomcat can read it.
- Let JavaScript sign without seeing the secret: non-extractable `CryptoKey`.
- Require personal approval: WebAuthn/passkey.
- Read/write protected plaintext: browser extension or native helper.

For Ed25519, use a non-extractable key instead of storing a readable password string.

> the important part i cant give up is that codex->bellsack.html->codex while the html is running multiple times live

You do not have to give that up.

A fast design requiring no stored password:

- Serve Bellsack HTML and JsEval.jsp from the same localhost origin.
- Remove all JsEval CORS headers.
- Remove executable query-string GETs.
- Codex sends raw JavaScript using HTTP PUT. Cross-origin webpages cannot send PUT without a successful CORS preflight.
- Bellsack keeps one waiting same-origin GET.
- Bellsack returns the raw result using same-origin POST.
- JSP rejects browser GET/POST unless `Sec-Fetch-Site` says `same-origin`.
- JSP rejects OPTIONS instead of granting CORS.

This preserves repeated live:

Codex → Bellsack → Codex → Bellsack → Codex

No timer, password, Ed25519, or extra hardware is needed. It protects against ordinary remote webpages impersonating you. It does not protect against malicious JavaScript already executing inside the trusted Bellsack tab, so the multiplayer/JsEval warning remains important.

> what if i just dont have cors headers in jseval

Removing JsEval CORS headers helps, but is not enough by itself.

CORS mainly prevents a remote webpage from reading responses. It does not prevent:

- Redirects
- Iframes
- Links
- Form POSTs
- Ordinary GET requests

Your current executable `JsEval.jsp?<code>` remains dangerous without CORS because navigation still sends it.

Minimum safe change:

- Remove CORS.
- Remove executable GET queries.
- Use PUT for Codex commands.
- Serve Bellsack from the same localhost origin so its GET/POST bridge still works.

> i cant put a password in every time i open the html

You would not need a password with the PUT/same-origin design.

Load Bellsack from Tomcat, remove JsEval CORS, and reserve PUT exclusively for Codex commands. Remote webpages cannot send that PUT without CORS permission.

So opening Bellsack remains automatic—no password entry or stored secret.

> i dont want to remove CORS cuz its supposed to be multiplayer game

Keep CORS in `BellsackServer*.jsp` for multiplayer.

Remove CORS only from `JsEval.jsp`, which is the local Codex-control bridge.

They are separate servers with separate security requirements, and your rule says they must not run together. Multiplayer CORS remains unchanged.

> thats what i meant on the jsps. but what about cors headers in the html. does that matter or is it only what the html calls out to

CORS headers on the HTML response do not grant the HTML permission to call other servers.

For an outbound Bellsack request:

- Bellsack makes the request.
- The target JSP’s response headers decide whether Bellsack may read it.

Therefore:

- `BellsackServer*.jsp` needs appropriate CORS because multiplayer Bellsack pages may call it from other origins.
- `JsEval.jsp` needs no CORS when Bellsack HTML is served from the same localhost origin.
- Bellsack HTML itself generally needs no CORS headers unless another origin must fetch and read the HTML file as data.

To restrict where the HTML can connect, use Content Security Policy `connect-src`; CORS does not do that.

> so JsEval.jsp will be localhost only, and BellsackServer.jsp will be anyone/cors

Yes.

- `JsEval.jsp`: localhost-only, no CORS, local Codex testing only.
- `BellsackServer*.jsp`: multiplayer-accessible with CORS, potentially reachable by anyone.

They must not be deployed or used together. Ideally, multiplayer CORS should allow only what its protocol requires.

> but JsEval is only 1 call. theres no "same server" to check

It is one logical Codex call, but currently uses multiple HTTP requests:

1. Bellsack has a waiting GET to `JsEval.jsp`.
2. Codex sends the JavaScript to `JsEval.jsp`.
3. JSP answers the waiting browser GET.
4. Bellsack POSTs the result.
5. JSP returns that result to Codex.

“Same origin” applies only to the Bellsack browser’s GET and POST. Codex’s command-line HTTP request is not subject to CORS.

Codex should choose strategy; local JS should handle moment-to-moment play.

> JsEvalCodexServer.jsp does not call any Codex or OpenAI API. It should be generalizable to near any AI

Correct. The JSP is AI-neutral string transport.

Any local agent with HTTP access can use it; cloud AIs need a local companion. The current JSP supports one active call, so five agents need separate local bridges or later multiplexing.

No changes made.

> design the json to be general:
> {type: "JsEvalCodexServer", msg: 'blah blah', ...}

Use one envelope:

`{type:"JsEvalCodexServer", version:1, op:"message", wantsResponse:true, msg:"blah blah"}`

Operations:

- `listen` — wait for incoming work
- `eval` — evaluate `msg` in browser
- `message` — send `msg` to the agent
- `result` — return `msg`

Keep `msg` always a string. The waiting HTTP request supplies correlation, so no ID is needed while only one call may be active. Add IDs only if later multiplexing concurrent calls.

> {type: "JsEvalCodexServer", msgsIn: ['blah blah'], msgsOut: ['other thing', 'hi codex'], ...}

Yes. Define direction relative to the browser:

`msgsIn`: agent → browser
`msgsOut`: browser → agent

Use FIFO ordering:

`{type:"JsEvalCodexServer", version:1, msgsIn:["code"], msgsOut:["result","message"]}`

This supports batching while keeping every payload a string. With one active exchange, no IDs are needed.

> call it msgsUp msgsDown for upload and download. calling what moves toward the browser as down and what moves toward codex/AI as up

Agreed:

`{type:"JsEvalCodexServer", version:1, msgsDown:["code for browser"], msgsUp:["message or result for AI"]}`

- `msgsDown`: Codex/AI → browser
- `msgsUp`: browser → Codex/AI

Direction is clear from the browser’s network perspective. No changes made.

> messages do not accumulate after being sent. its just if u have multiple things to do at once

Right. They are ephemeral batch fields, not logs:

- Hold only currently pending messages.
- Deliver the whole array once.
- Clear it immediately after delivery.
- Empty arrays mean nothing moving that direction.
- Multiple entries mean “do these together,” not accumulated history.

> you only send this data format with msgsUp empty or msgsDown empty, not both

> so its gonna be secure against non-localhost trickery (iframe to localhost in someone elses website for example) being able to message to my localhost codex?

Yes—against that specific attack, once implemented and tested.

A hostile website may still make the browser contact localhost, but its request will be rejected because:

- Only `POST` is accepted.
- `Origin` must exactly equal `http://localhost:8080`.
- `Sec-Fetch-Site` must equal `same-origin`.
- `Host` must exactly match `localhost:8080`.
- The network peer must be loopback.
- No private-endpoint CORS is provided.

This does not protect against malicious JavaScript already running on the same localhost origin, hostile local programs, browser extensions, or a reverse proxy masking remote clients as loopback. The redesign is not implemented yet.

> Do u think this is a good security design?

It is a good defense against hostile websites contacting localhost. It fails closed and correctly uses POST, exact Origin/Host, Fetch Metadata, loopback checks, and no CORS.

But it is not complete authentication. Two important gaps remain:

- Every page/script on `http://localhost:8080` shares the trusted origin, regardless of path.
- The authorized-launcher-to-specific-tab handoff is not yet proven.

For strong security, the private bridge should have its own origin/port and a per-launch, memory-only capability established by the authorized launcher. Without that, I’d call it good CSRF protection, not complete identity proof.

`Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin`

The JSP requires that exact browser-controlled header. A remote webpage targeting localhost should send `cross-site`, not `same-origin`.

It also requires:

`Origin: http://localhost:8080`

> yes. is JsEvalCodexServer.jsp emitting Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin? And is the bat emitting Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin?

Neither emits it directly.

- `JsEvalCodexServer.jsp` checks that incoming `Sec-Fetch-Site` equals `same-origin`.
- The BAT only opens Bellsack.
- Chrome automatically adds `Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin` when that localhost Bellsack page POSTs to the same localhost origin.

JavaScript cannot manually set that protected header.

> the bat doesnt need to emit it. my bad.

Right. The BAT only opens the same-origin page. Chrome supplies the protected header on the page’s JSP requests.

The JSP gate is: localhost + POST + exact Origin + `Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin` + mode headers.

> but when codex calls curl or whatever it does

When Codex calls the JSP directly with curl/PowerShell, Codex must explicitly add:

- `Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin`
- `Origin: http://localhost:8080`
- both mode headers
- JSON `Content-Type`

Native local programs can spoof these headers. They protect against remote webpages, not malicious local software.

- The normal boot/FPS report was replaced by a temporary JSP report.
- Bridge startup moved late, so it cannot report early startup crashes.
- The download button downloads the source file, not live runtime edits.
- Multiple simultaneous live tabs currently collide.

My recommendation: keep the architecture, but clean up the contradictory authorization wording, dependency declaration, temporary report, and startup timing before merging. The security model should honestly say `codexLive=1` is a local mode switch—not authentication.

> - Ran `rg -n -e 'evalJsCodeFromCodex' -e 'evalOne' -e 'messageType==="eval"' -e 'JsEvalCodexServer\.[A-Za-z]+' 'J:\q\Q63x\w\bellsack\codex06XX\Bellsack06XX.html' | Select-Object -First 100`

Codex starts the `eval` operation:

`Codex → messageType:"eval" → browser evalOne(code) → messageType:"evalResult" → Codex`

It currently has no exported function name. The old name was `BS.evalJsCodeFromCodex(string)`.

> i dont see evalJsCodeFromCodex. what did u rename it to

I replaced it with the internal function `evalOne(code)`.

Codex triggers it by sending a `messageType: "eval"` envelope. It is not currently exported as `JsEvalCodexServer.evalJsCodeFromCodex`.

> wtf is let value=(0,eval)(code);

It is indirect global `eval`.

`(0, eval)` evaluates to the built-in `eval` function, then `(code)` calls it indirectly. Therefore the code runs in global scope, where it can access `BS`, `q`, `Lamgl`, etc., but not `evalOne`’s local variables.

Equivalent clearer spelling:

`globalThis.eval(code)`

> why wouldnt you just eval(code)

Because `eval(code)` is direct eval. It can see `evalOne`’s private local variables and closure state.

`(0,eval)(code)` runs globally, more like the browser console. That keeps live code from depending on or accidentally modifying bridge internals.

> did you make another eval func

No. `evalOne(code)` is only a wrapper around JavaScript’s built-in global `eval`. It adds logging, string conversion, and error handling.

> so this other func you're trying not to call dcoesnt exist

Correct. There is no separate public function anymore.

`BS.evalJsCodeFromCodex` was removed. Codex sends an `eval` protocol message, and the private `evalOne(code)` handles it. I described it confusingly.
